title: Mechanics Foundations — Original Internal Assessment Draft Pack

items.learningObjective: Explain the relativity of rest and motion by comparing passenger observations from train and platform frames.
items.stem: A train is moving along a straight horizontal track at a constant speed of $20\text{ m/s}$. A passenger sitting inside the train carriage places a book on their tray table. Which of the following statements correctly describes the state of motion of the book?
options: A. The book is strictly at absolute rest because it does not change its position on the tray table.
B. The book is at rest relative to the train carriage, but moving at $20\text{ m/s}$ relative to an observer standing stationary on the platform.
C. The book is moving at $20\text{ m/s}$ relative to both the carriage tray table and the stationary platform observer.
D. The book cannot be considered at rest relative to any observer since the Earth itself is rotating.
items.signConvention: Positive in the direction of train motion.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: The passenger's frame of reference moves at 20 m/s relative to the ground. The book has zero velocity relative to the passenger (at rest) but has a velocity equal to the train relative to the ground observer (20 m/s). Rest and motion are frame-dependent.
items.criticalErrors: Believing motion is absolute or that platform is the only correct reference frame.
items.commonFailureSignals: Choosing Option A due to assuming 'at rest' only means zero velocity relative to the immediate surroundings.

items.learningObjective: Distinguish between total path distance and straight-line displacement in a 1D turn-back scenario.
items.stem: An object starts at position $x = +5\text{ m}$ on a one-dimensional coordinate axis. It moves along the axis to $x = +15\text{ m}$, turns back, and moves to $x = -2\text{ m}$. What are the total distance traveled and the net displacement of the object during this motion?
options: A. Distance = 27 m, Displacement = -7 m
B. Distance = 27 m, Displacement = +7 m
C. Distance = 17 m, Displacement = -7 m
D. Distance = 17 m, Displacement = +7 m
items.givenData: Initial position = +5 m, Intermediate position = +15 m, Final position = -2 m.
items.diagramSpecification: 1D coordinate axis schematic indicating the turnaround point.
items.signConvention: Positive x-axis points to the right.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Path 1: From +5 m to +15 m is +10 m. Path 2: From +15 m to -2 m is 17 m in the negative direction. Total distance = 10 m + 17 m = 27 m. Net displacement = x_f - x_i = -2 m - 5 m = -7 m.
items.criticalErrors: Confusing distance with displacement magnitude or summing them directly without direction.
items.commonFailureSignals: Selecting C or D due to equating displacement magnitude with distance, or subtracting final position absolute values.

items.learningObjective: Calculate average speed and average velocity vector for a two-segment 1D motion where the object reverses direction.
items.stem: A runner moves along a straight $x$-axis in the positive direction from $x = 0$ to $x = +100\text{ m}$ in $40\text{ s}$, then turns around and runs in the negative direction from $x = +100\text{ m}$ to $x = +70\text{ m}$ in $10\text{ s}$. Calculate the magnitude of the runner's average velocity and the runner's average speed over the entire $50\text{ s}$ interval, in $\text{m/s}$. Enter the magnitude of average velocity first, followed by average speed, separated by a comma (e.g., 2.3, 3.4).
options: NOT_APPLICABLE
items.responseConstraints: Numeric values only, rounded to one decimal place, separated by a single comma.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Total time = 40 + 10 = 50 s. Net displacement = 70 - 0 = 70 m. Average velocity magnitude = 70 m / 50 s = 1.4 m/s. Total distance = 100 m + 30 m = 130 m. Average speed = 130 m / 50 s = 2.6 m/s.
items.acceptableResponseEvidence: Exact string match: '1.4, 2.6' or with single space '1.4, 2.6'.
items.criticalErrors: Claiming average speed and velocity are identical, or averaging the rates directly.
items.commonFailureSignals: Entering identical values for both velocity and speed (e.g. 2.6, 2.6).

items.learningObjective: Explain that a negative velocity indicates direction of motion in 1D rather than magnitude changes.
items.stem: A particle's motion is restricted to a straight horizontal line where the positive direction points to the right. At a certain instant, the particle has a velocity of $-8\text{ m/s}$ and an acceleration of $-3\text{ m/s}^2$. Which of the following statements about the particle's motion at this instant are correct? Select all options that apply.
options: A. The particle is moving to the left.
B. The particle is slowing down because its velocity is negative.
C. The particle is speeding up.
D. The particle's acceleration is directed to the left.
items.signConvention: Right is positive, left is negative.
items.unitsRequirement: Velocity in m/s, acceleration in m/s^2.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Negative velocity indicates motion is in the negative direction (left -> A is correct). Negative acceleration indicates acceleration vector points to the left (-> D is correct). Since velocity and acceleration vectors point in the same direction (both left/negative), the speed of the particle is increasing (-> C is correct).
items.acceptableResponseEvidence: Selection of options A, C, and D.
items.criticalErrors: Selecting B (believing negative velocity always means slowing down) or claiming velocity/acceleration oppose each other.
items.noncriticalErrors: Missing one of the correct choices.
items.commonFailureSignals: Selecting A and B under the assumption that negative velocity represents deceleration.

items.learningObjective: Determine whether an object is stationary, moving forward, or reversing by analyzing the position-time (x-t) graph slope.
items.stem: A position-time ($x-t$) graph depicts the motion of two objects, A and B, along a straight line. Object A is represented by a steep straight line starting at $x = 0$ at $t = 0$ and reaching $x = 10\text{ m}$ at $t = 2\text{ s}$. Object B is represented by a horizontal flat line at $x = 20\text{ m}$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 5\text{ s}$. What are the velocities of Object A and Object B during the interval $t = 0$ to $t = 2\text{ s}$?
options: A. Velocity of A = 5 m/s, Velocity of B = 0 m/s
B. Velocity of A = 10 m/s, Velocity of B = 20 m/s
C. Velocity of A = 5 m/s, Velocity of B = 10 m/s
D. Velocity of A = 0 m/s, Velocity of B = 20 m/s
items.givenData: Object A line coordinates: (0, 0) to (2, 10). Object B coordinates: horizontal line at x=20.
items.diagramSpecification: A graph showing x (meters) on the vertical axis and t (seconds) on the horizontal axis. Line A goes from origin to (2, 10), Line B is flat at y=20.
items.unitsRequirement: Position in m, time in s, velocity in m/s.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Velocity is the slope of the position-time graph. Slope of A = (10 - 0) / 2 = 5 m/s. Slope of B (horizontal line) = 0 m/s. Note: Target B has a higher vertical position (20 m) but its speed is zero.
items.partialCreditAnchors: 1 point awarded if the student correctly calculates slope of A but misinterprets B.
items.criticalErrors: Treating y-axis height as speed (selecting options with B velocity = 20 m/s).
items.commonFailureSignals: Selecting B because B's line is 'higher' on the graph.

items.learningObjective: Calculate acceleration and displacement from the slope and signed area of a velocity-time (v-t) graph.
items.stem: A velocity-time ($v-t$) graph of a toy car moving along a straight line starts at $(0, 0)$. It rises linearly to $(4, +8\text{ m/s})$, remains constant at $+8\text{ m/s}$ until $t = 6\text{ s}$, and then drops linearly to zero at $t = 10\text{ s}$. What is the acceleration of the toy car between $t = 6\text{ s}$ and $t = 10\text{ s}$, and what is its net displacement over the entire $10\text{ s}$ motion?
options: A. Acceleration = -2 m/s^2, Net Displacement = 56 m
B. Acceleration = -2 m/s^2, Net Displacement = 48 m
C. Acceleration = +2 m/s^2, Net Displacement = 56 m
D. Acceleration = -8 m/s^2, Net Displacement = 48 m
items.diagramSpecification: A graph showing v (in m/s) on the vertical axis and t (in s) on the horizontal axis, plotting three segments: positive slope, flat, negative slope.
items.unitsRequirement: Displacement in meters (m), acceleration in m/s^2.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Acceleration is slope of v-t: slope = (0 - 8)/(10 - 6) = -2 m/s^2. Displacement is the area under v-t curve: Area of trapezoid = 0.5 * (2 + 10) * 8 = 48 m.
items.partialCreditAnchors: 1 point awarded if acceleration is calculated correctly but displacement is wrong (or vice versa).
items.criticalErrors: Treating displacement as simple distance summation without sign or confusing slope with area.
items.commonFailureSignals: Selecting A due to incorrect calculation of trapezoid side lengths.

items.learningObjective: Define constant acceleration and explain how velocity can be zero momentarily while acceleration is non-zero.
items.stem: A ball is thrown straight upward into the air. At the highest point of its flight, the ball is momentarily at rest. Explain whether the ball's acceleration at this highest point is zero or non-zero, and state the condition under which the standard kinematic equations (constant-acceleration equations) can be used to describe this motion.
options: NOT_APPLICABLE
items.responseConstraints: Provide a short paragraph answer (maximum 3 sentences).
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Even when velocity is zero momentarily at the peak, it is changing from upward to downward, so acceleration is non-zero. The standard kinematic equations require that the acceleration is constant in both magnitude and direction during the entire motion.
items.provisionalKeyCandidate: Acceleration is non-zero because the velocity is changing. Kinematic equations require constant acceleration.
items.acceptableResponseEvidence: Explanation must state that acceleration is non-zero and that equations apply only if acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction.
items.criticalErrors: Asserting that acceleration must be zero because velocity is zero.
items.commonFailureSignals: Claiming acceleration is zero at the top because the ball is not moving.

items.learningObjective: Select the correct kinematic equation for constant acceleration based on given/find parameters.
items.stem:
Match the given set of physical parameters for a constant acceleration motion to the most appropriate kinematic equation to find the required unknown directly in one step.
Parameters:
1. Given: initial velocity ($u$), acceleration ($a$), time interval ($t$). Find: final velocity ($v$).
2. Given: initial velocity ($u$), final velocity ($v$), displacement ($s$). Find: acceleration ($a$).
3. Given: initial velocity ($u$), acceleration ($a$), displacement ($s$). Find: time interval ($t$).
Equations:
X: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$
Y: $v = u + at$
Z: $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$
items.givenData: Three parameter scenarios and three equation choices.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Scenario 1 contains u, a, t, v. The equation linking these is v = u + at (Y). Scenario 2 contains u, v, s, a. The equation is v^2 = u^2 + 2as (X). Scenario 3 contains u, a, s, t. The equation is s = ut + 0.5 * a * t^2 (Z).
items.criticalErrors: Selecting equations that contain multiple unknown variables.

items.learningObjective: Execute a multi-step calculation using UAM equations and perform a dimensional/sanity check.
items.stem: Two spheres, Sphere 1 of mass $1\text{ kg}$ and Sphere 2 of mass $5\text{ kg}$, are dropped from rest from the top of a tower. Both spheres experience the exact same constant downward acceleration of $10\text{ m/s}^2$ throughout their fall. Calculate the distance in meters traveled by Sphere 2 during the first $3.0\text{ s}$ of its fall. Enter the numeric value only, rounded to one decimal place. (Note: The motion is strictly one-dimensional, where downward is defined as positive.)
options: NOT_APPLICABLE
items.responseConstraints: Numeric value only, rounded to one decimal place. Do not include units.
items.givenData: Mass of Sphere 1 = 1 kg, Mass of Sphere 2 = 5 kg, Initial speed u = 0, constant acceleration a = 10 m/s^2, time t = 3.0 s.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: The equation for displacement is s = ut + 0.5 * a * t^2. Substituting u = 0, a = 10 m/s^2, and t = 3.0 s: s = 0 + 0.5 * 10 * (3.0)^2 = 45.0 m. Mass does not appear in kinematic equations, so Sphere 2's mass of 5 kg does not change its acceleration or distance.
items.partialCreditAnchors: 1 point awarded if the calculation is setup correctly but contains a basic math arithmetic error.
items.criticalErrors: Multiplying or dividing the kinematic result by mass (e.g. scaling by 5 to get 225), demonstrating the heavier-object misconception.
items.commonFailureSignals: Entering 225.0 due to multiplying displacement by mass.

items.learningObjective: Explain Newton's First Law and identify that constant velocity implies zero net force.
items.stem: A deep-space probe is traveling through a frictionless region of space far from any gravitational source. It is moving in a straight line at a constant velocity of $1200\text{ m/s}$. Which of the following statements correctly describes the net force acting on the probe?
options: A. A constant net force must act in the direction of motion to maintain this velocity.
B. The net force acting on the probe is exactly zero.
C. A net force opposing the motion must exist to prevent the probe from speeding up.
D. The net force must be non-zero since the probe has momentum.
items.givenData: Frictionless environment, constant velocity v = 1200 m/s.
criticalGateIds: zero net force under Newton's First Law
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Newton's First Law states that an object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force. Since velocity is constant (a = 0), the net force acting on the probe must be zero. No force is required to sustain motion.
items.criticalErrors: Believing that a forward force is required to keep an object moving.
items.commonFailureSignals: Selecting A because of the high velocity.

items.learningObjective: Relate an object's mass to its translational inertia and compare the resistance to changes in motion.
items.stem: Two blocks, Block X of mass $2\text{ kg}$ and Block Y of mass $10\text{ kg}$, are placed side-by-side on a frictionless horizontal ice surface. A student attempts to push each block from rest to a speed of $2\text{ m/s}$. Which block has greater inertia, and how is inertia correctly interpreted here?
options: A. Block Y has greater inertia because it has more mass; inertia is its resistance to acceleration.
B. Block Y has greater inertia because it exerts a larger active inertia force to oppose the push.
C. Both blocks have the same inertia because they are on the same frictionless surface.
D. Block X has greater inertia because it is easier to accelerate.
items.givenData: Mass of Block X = 2 kg, Mass of Block Y = 10 kg, final speed = 2 m/s.
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Inertia is an inherent property of matter that quantifies its resistance to changes in motion (acceleration). Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia. Block Y has greater mass (10 kg vs 2 kg), so it has greater inertia. Inertia is not an active force vector.
items.criticalErrors: Modeling inertia as a force vector.
items.commonFailureSignals: Selecting B under the impression that inertia is an opposing force.

items.learningObjective: Analyze an integrated scenario containing a constant velocity segment and a constant acceleration segment, verifying correct force-motion mapping.
items.stem: A hovercraft of mass $m = 100\text{ kg}$ moves along a straight line on a frictionless track. Its velocity-time ($v-t$) graph consists of two phases: Phase 1 (from $t = 0$ to $5\text{ s}$): a horizontal flat line at $v = +4\text{ m/s}$. Phase 2 (from $t = 5\text{ s}$ to $10\text{ s}$): a straight line with a constant slope, decreasing from $+4\text{ m/s}$ to $0\text{ m/s}$. Analyze the net horizontal force acting on the hovercraft during Phase 1 and Phase 2. Connect your reasoning to Newton's First Law and explain the role of inertia. (Do not perform calculations using Newton's Second Law.)
options: NOT_APPLICABLE
items.givenData: Hovercraft mass = 100 kg, frictionless track. Phase 1 velocity = +4 m/s (constant). Phase 2 velocity decreases from +4 to 0 m/s linearly.
items.requiredRepresentation: qualitative force diagram reasoning, velocity-time graph
items.diagramSpecification: A sketch of the v-t graph and two qualitative force-arrow diagrams (one for Phase 1 showing balanced arrows, one for Phase 2 showing a backward net force).
items.signConvention: Positive x-direction is the direction of initial velocity.
criticalGateIds: zero net force under Newton's First Law
items.expectedReasoningOutline: Phase 1: Velocity is constant, so acceleration is zero. By Newton's First Law, the net horizontal force is exactly zero. No horizontal force is required to sustain this motion. Phase 2: Velocity is decreasing linearly, indicating a constant negative acceleration. Therefore, a non-zero, constant net horizontal force must act in the direction opposite to motion. Inertia is the hovercraft's resistance (due to its 100 kg mass) to this change in motion, causing it to glide forward during the deceleration phase rather than stopping instantaneously.
items.provisionalKeyCandidate: Phase 1 has zero net force due to constant velocity (First Law). Phase 2 has a non-zero opposing net force causing deceleration. Inertia of the 100 kg mass resists this change.
items.acceptableResponseEvidence: Must explicitly state that net force in Phase 1 is zero, Phase 2 net force is non-zero (opposing), and describe inertia as resistance to acceleration rather than a force.
items.partialCreditAnchors: 1 point awarded if forces are correctly mapped but inertia is incorrectly described.
items.criticalErrors: Recommending a forward net force for Phase 1 or labeling inertia as an active force vector.
items.commonFailureSignals: Stating a forward force is needed in Phase 1 to maintain the speed.
